feedback: If a line is drawn through categorical data (joining bars that shouldn't be joined), point out that these points aren't connected — sort the data as categories versus continuous first, then re-choose the graph type before drawing.
If the scale is spaced by the order the numbers were collected rather than by value, note that equal gaps must mean equal amounts; mark the whole axis before plotting any point.

If the scale squashes the data into a corner, suggest using fewer units per square so the data fills the grid and any pattern is easier to see; on a bar chart, keep the count axis starting at zero so the bar heights can still be compared fairly.
If axes carry numbers but no quantity name or unit, require each axis to name what was measured and its unit before the graph is 'finished'; check against the data-table headings.
Ask: why did you pick this graph type rather than a bar chart / line graph for this data? If someone else read it, would they know what each axis measures and in what units — show me where.
activities.intendedInsight: A graph isn't a decoration added at the end — the right choice of type, axes and scale is what lets the data tell its story, while the wrong one can hide the pattern or imply connections that don't exist.
learnerActions: Take a real dataset — ideally from your own fair test (e.g. a plant's height measured each week) — plus a categorical set (e.g. favourite-fruit counts) and a two-variable set.

Decide for each dataset whether the data is categorical, a continuous variable tracked as it changes over time (or as another continuous variable changes), or two measured continuous variables checked for a relationship.

Choose the graph type: bar chart for categories, line graph for a continuous variable tracked as it changes over time (or as another continuous variable changes), scatter graph for two measured continuous variables where you are looking for a relationship.

Put the changed/independent variable (or the categories, for a bar chart) on the x-axis and the measured/dependent variable on the y-axis; if a scatter graph compares two measured variables and neither was changed, choose one for each axis and say which. Label each axis with the quantity AND its unit where it has one.

Mark the scale on each numerical axis FIRST — equal squares for equal amounts — choosing a scale that spreads the data across the grid rather than squashing it into a corner; on a bar chart, space the categories evenly and start the count axis at zero.
Plot each point accurately (read the value, find the coordinate, mark precisely), then check by reading one point back off the graph against the data table.

Deliberately try plotting the categorical data as a line graph and notice that the joining lines suggest in-between values that don't exist, and that the line's shape changes if you reorder the categories; compare with the correct bar chart.
activities.title: Plot your own data: choosing type, axes and scale

feedback: If questions are vague or non-binary, or two organisms end at the same point, rework them: every question must be an observable yes/no that divides the remaining set.
Prompt: run this organism through your key — does every question have a clear yes or no answer? What happens if two look the same?
activities.intendedInsight: A working key is built from clear, binary, observable distinctions that divide a set until every specimen is uniquely identified.
learnerActions: Take a small set of organisms (or specimens) to sort by observable features.
Write a sequence of yes/no questions, each about an observable feature, that splits the remaining set at every step.
Draw the key as a branching structure so each organism reaches its own endpoint.
Test the key by running every organism through it, checking that each question has a clear yes or no answer and that no two organisms end at the same point.
If two specimens look the same at a step, add a finer observable question that separates them.
activities.title: Build and test a classification key
